title: ChronoSurv: A Clinical Pathway-Guided Graph Framework for Multimodal Survival Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: ChronoSurv introduces a novel clinical pathway-guided multimodal fusion strategy by explicitly modeling patient trajectories from patient background to cancer diagnosis and surgical intervention. The experimental setup is well designed, including a wide range of conventional non-deep learning and deep learning survival analysis methods, as well as state-of-the-art multimodal deep learning models, evaluated across multiple public head and neck cancer datasets. ChronoSurv enables progression-wise interpretation of the clinical trajectory, thereby allowing the model to capture stage-specific contributions of different modalities to survival prediction.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: This work aims to represent a progression-aware clinical trajectory using a hierarchical directed graph. However, the implementation details of this trajectory are insufficiently specified in the main text. In Section 2.2, the authors introduce three key clinical steps—(1) patient background, (2) initial cancer diagnosis, and (3) local surgery—but do not explicitly specify how individual sub-modalities (e. g. , clinical, history, pathology) are assigned to these steps. Clarifying how sub-modalities are assigned to each clinical step would improve the reproducibility of the proposed framework. The performance improvements reported in Table 2 appear to be relatively marginal compared to the benchmark methods. In particular, given that the evaluation is based on a single 5-fold cross-validation and small dataset sizes, it is difficult to consider the reproducible results. Providing additional evaluation, such as reporting statistical significance (e. g. , Wilcoxon rank-sum test), would strengthen the validity of the results. There is no mention or description of Fig. 2(c) (Example of prediction) in the main text. Several details necessary for reproducibility are missing: The architecture of the survival head is not described. In the component-wise ablation study, it is unclear how the model aggregates the Level 2 step nodes in the w/o level 3 setting. While it appears that a simple pooling operation may have been used, this is not explicitly stated. Such details are important for ensuring reproducibility. Corrections: In Table 2, the best C-index for the TCGA-HNSC dataset is achieved by HFBSurv (. 660). In Table 3, the best C-index for the TCGA-HNSC dataset is achieved by Cross-attention (. 656). In Table 4, the best IBS for the TCGA-HNSC dataset is achieved by the w/o heterogeneity setting (. 179).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors tackle an important problem, namely the use of multiple modalities, tacking into account the temporal processes and dependencies characteristic for time-to-event data. The use of (directed) GNNs is conceptually useful in this context. The design of the model and its application follow current developments in the respective areas (i.e. heterogeneous convolutions rather than late fusion, etc.). Patient-specific graph topology is a good idea. The article is well written, easy to follow and for the most part technically sound. Results are presented clearly and the ablation study is well done.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are two main limitations/concerns for this paper: 1) As is typical for time-to-event data (especially for the type of analysis pursued here, i.e. multi-modal data with images) the availability of data is a recurring problem: There are few suitable data sets and the ones available have small sample sizes, and worse, small number of events, 763 * .72(censoring) * .15 (test set) = 82 events in the test set for the big data set, which hinders generalization. The results table is also a bit misleading. UniHNC looks like a separate data point but is in fact a weighted average of the other two, with the HANCOCK data being the bigger one and the only one where the model outperforms SurvPCG. So the overall evidence for improvement is not too overwhelming. Altough I should stress that I don’t care about showing that the model outperforms competitors. Null-results (more or less) are fine, but the presentation and honest result description is important. 2) Level two clinical steps seem to be an important driver of the performance, but this step is not explained clearly and is crucial to understand temporal dependencies and the nature of the problem. a) Why do some level one parameters connect to step 2, but not step 1 and 3 and vice versa? is this based on how these are applied accross time? b) there is also a directed progression from step1 -> step3 and step1->step2->step3. The authors need to explain the arrow of time better, i.e. at which time the respective information is available fro prediction. When does the observation start (time-origin) and at which time-points are the information about the individual steps given and what is the end-point (death?). My concern is that some of the steps are only known after baseline, for example t=0 -> start of observation, t=10 -> surgery, t=11 -> death. Using info about surgery at t=10 would imply that event cannot have happened beforehand (immortal time bias). Using such time-dependent features is a totally different task then predicting from baseline (without taking future information into account) and the method then should be compared to models with same amount of information (e.g. time-dependent Cox, dynamic DeepHit, …). Authors should clarify if that is the case here and reformulate to make clear that this is not the case otherwise.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clinically grounded modeling: The explicit alignment of the graph structure with the clinical care pathway (background → diagnosis → surgery) introduces domain knowledge into the model design, improving interpretability and plausibility. Principled handling of missing modalities: Missing data are addressed by removing nodes and edges from the graph, avoiding imputation or masking heuristics and yielding a clean and adaptive formulation. Hierarchical representation learning: The multi-level graph enables structured aggregation from fine-grained to global representations, which is well-supported by ablation results. Heterogeneous message passing: Relation-specific transformations allow modeling asymmetric and semantically different interactions (e.g., modality-to-step vs. temporal dependencies). Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation includes multiple datasets (HANCOCK, TCGA-HNSC, UniHNC), cross-validation, and comparison with classical, deep, and multimodal baselines. Calibration analysis: Inclusion of calibration metrics and D-calibration testing strengthens the evaluation beyond standard discrimination metrics. Detailed ablation study: Systematic removal of graph components (steps, hierarchy, directionality, heterogeneity) provides strong evidence of the contribution of each design choice.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Hand-crafted graph topology: The clinical pathway (three steps) is predefined and fixed, which may limit scalability and adaptability to other diseases or clinical workflows. Simplified temporal modeling: The clinical trajectory is reduced to three discrete steps, which may not capture the complexity and variability of real-world patient pathways. Limited modality diversity: Although multimodal, the evaluation is restricted to specific combinations (WSI, tabular, text), with no experiments on broader imaging modalities (e.g., CT, MRI) or more diverse clinical settings. No analysis of computational complexity: The cost of graph construction and heterogeneous message passing is not discussed, especially compared to simpler fusion baselines. Limited treatment of missing modalities: Although the method adapts the graph topology by removing nodes corresponding to missing modalities, it does not explicitly model missingness mechanisms (e.g., MCAR/MAR/MNAR) nor evaluate robustness under different missing data patterns. This limits the understanding of its behavior in realistic clinical scenarios where missingness is often structured and non-random.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Reviewers [R] and the Meta-Reviewer [MR] for their valuable feedback. We address the main concerns below: [R2, MR] Arrow of time / fair comparison. We agree that the prediction setting must be clarified. ChronoSurv is not intended as a first-consultation model. It is a static prognosis model using information available from the index clinical workup. Importantly, ChronoSurv and all 11 competing methods in Table 2 receive the identical input feature set under the same preprocessing. In both HANCOCK and TCGA-HNSC, t=0 is the date of initial pathologic diagnosis, following each benchmark’s standard survival convention. Diagnostic workup-derived variables (e.g., primary tumor FFPE WSIs typically acquired at resection) enter as static workup observations rather than time-dependent covariates: a standard practice in multimodal oncologic survival analysis, mirroring the canonical treatment of post-surgical pTNM as static despite its post-resection acquisition. Surgery typically occurs soon after diagnosis (mean ~36 days in UniHNC vs. ~1215 days mean time to last information), making the workup window short relative to the observation period. This workup-window effect therefore reflects a limitation of the standard retrospective benchmark formulation, shared identically by all models, rather than future information uniquely exploited by ChronoSurv. Furthermore, the directed edges in ChronoSurv encode the clinical order of feature acquisition during workup, not follow-up evolution. No timestamp info (e.g., surgery date) is used as model input. Time-dependent follow-up features (e.g., recurrence, progression) are deliberately excluded. Extension to dynamic graphs for longitudinal survival analysis, with comparison against time-dependent models (e.g., time-dependent Cox), is left for future work. [R1, R2, R3] Clinical-step assignment. Sub-modality -> step mapping is deterministic (Fig. 1b). Step 1: Background (age, sex, smoking status). Step 2: Clinical (e.g., primary site, metastasis at diagnosis), Blood (38 analytes), History (text). Step 3: Pathology (e.g., post-surgical pTNM, grade, invasion, margins), WSIs (primary tumor + lymph-node), Surgery (reports + description). Each leaf is embedded (Sec. 2.1) and linked by directed edges (Sec. 2.2). Topology may be adapted to other diseases, but our contribution is the framework: a generalizable clinical pathway-guided survival graph. [R1, R2, MR] Data limitations & statistical validation. We acknowledge the limited cohort sizes and event counts in public HNC benchmarks. UniHNC is HANCOCK+TCGA-HNSC, not an independent dataset (will be clarified in Sec. 3). Despite these limitations, ChronoSurv achieves competitive performance across folds with per-fold std reported in Table 2: best-or-tied IBS, competitive C-index values, and consistent D-Calibration test (5/5 folds vs. SurvPCG 1/5). [R3, MR] Computational complexity. End-to-end inference (graph construction + heterogeneous message passing) takes ~30 ms/sample on an RTX 2080 Ti, enabling clinical deployment. The GNN forward pass adds negligible cost on top of the (frozen) feature extractors shared with baselines. [R1, R2] Survival predictions + risk score. Survival from hazards: S(t_j|X) = prod_{k=1..j} (1 - lambda(t_k|X)). The Fig. 2c estimate is the restricted mean T_hat = sum_{t=0..T_max} S_hat(t). Per-patient risk is -T_hat, with the Uno C-index [33]. We will reference Fig. 2c in Sec. 3.3 and cite Gensheimer & Narasimhan (2019). [R3] Missing modality analysis. Missingness is heterogeneous: curation gaps or selective analytes (e.g., CRP [15]). ChronoSurv does not explicitly model missingness mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) but handles them via adaptive topology. [R1] Reproducibility. Survival head: 3-layer MLP + sigmoid producing per-bin hazards. w/o-level-3 ablation: step-2 nodes mean-pooled before the head. Table 2-4 highlights will be corrected.

One main issue is potential bias from the arrow of time and unfair model comparisons (e.g., immortal time, time-dependent features), which would warrant rejection if justified; they also note a missing analysis of computational complexity. | After reviewing the comments and the authors’ responses, I find that the main concerns have been addressed. Overall, the paper is in good shape for acceptance. I recommend accepting the submission, while encouraging the authors to incorporate the reviewers’ suggestions carefully when preparing the final version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper proposes a clinical pathway-guided graph framework for multimodal survival analysis. Reviewers appreciate the clinically motivated graph design. However, after rebuttal, key concern remains regarding the arrow of time in the survival prediction setting and whether post-baseline information may introduce bias or give the proposed model an unfair advantage. The rebuttal clarifies the intended static prognosis setting and addresses several reproducibility details, but it does not fully resolve the concern about temporal validity and fair comparison, especially given the small datasets and limited statistical validation. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The main concern is the unresolved arrow-of-time issue: some surgery/pathology features appear to be acquired after the baseline time origin, which may introduce immortal time bias or future-information leakage. This directly affects the validity of the survival prediction setting and the fairness of comparison. Although the framework is clinically interesting, the rebuttal does not fully eliminate this concern, and the evidence is not sufficient for acceptance.

title: CPAgents: Agentic Composite Phenotype Generation for Cardiac Disease Association
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper’s key strengths are its structured agentic framework for feature discovery, combining statistical analysis with LLM-guided generation, and its focus on interpretable, closed-form phenotypes. It includes a robust multi-stage validation process and a comprehensive evaluation across diseases and models, demonstrating consistent performance gains and practical relevance on large-scale clinical data.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: A key weakness is limited conceptual novelty. The overall pipeline closely resembles prior work on LLM-driven feature engineering and symbolic composition, such as LLM-FE (Abhyankar et al. , 2025) and agent-based systems like MESHAgents (Zhang et al. , 2025). The Analyst–Proposer–Verifier loop is intuitive but not clearly differentiated from existing multi-agent or symbolic regression frameworks.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The analyse–propose–verify decomposition is clean and better scoped than most LLM-FE work. Grounding the Proposer with Analyst statistics (ΔAIC, MI, ICC) is a meaningful design choice. 2.The evaluation is large-scale and leakage-aware. A 6:2:2 split with discovery restricted to train+val, five seeds, and bootstrap stability selection show care. 3.The 72-configuration ranking analysis avoids cherry-picking. The silhouette score, association heatmap, and agent-level ablation triangulate the core claim well. Which deserves credit. 4.The sex-stratified allometric LVM Z-score example is a convincing demonstration that LLM medical priors can surface genuinely clinical constants. This is really intuitive.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I would like to have few clarifications from the authors regarding- 1.Gains are small and often within overlapping standard deviations. SVM Hypertension is 0.759±0.006 vs 0.755±0.007.No paired significance tests (DeLong, bootstrap, Wilcoxon) are reported to back the 56 vs 18 ranking claim. Can you do the paired-significance tests and report the results in your rebuttal? 2.I think a compariosn with non-LLM AutoFE methods (OpenFE, AutoFeat, featuretools) or a random search over the same operator set O could be really intuitive to observe. Without these, the LLM’s contribution cannot be isolated from the AST pipeline itself. The ablation already removes agents but never the LLM. 3.LLM reproducibility is unclear. Results use DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5.1 at default temperature. The five-seed averaging does not isolate LLM stochasticity from classifier seed variance. A temperature-0 run would help. While working on LLMs, I think this is necessary to report in the results table.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: A major strength of the paper is its emphasis on interpretable composite phenotypes, moving beyond single imaging measurements toward higher‑level constructs that better reflect cardiovascular disease complexity. This aligns well with clinical reasoning and phenome‑wide study objectives. A second strength is the agent‑based formulation, where analysis, synthesis, and verification are explicitly separated, providing built‑in quality control and reducing manual, ad‑hoc feature engineering.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The is the use of the term “phenome‑wide association study” without performing any actual association analysis, particularly genetic associations, which may lead to conceptual ambiguity under traditional PheWAS definitions. Second, the framework operates exclusively on pre‑extracted imaging features, inheriting any biases or limitations of upstream steps. Third, while statistically well motivated, the proposed criteria for phenotype construction are not explicitly grounded in pathophysiological or clinical priors, leaving the clinical meaningfulness of some composite phenotypes to be inferred rather than demonstrated.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are pleased that the reviewers recognised CPAgents as a compelling framework for clinical reasoning, highlighting its “clean analyse-propose-verify decomposition” (R1, R2), “interpretable composite phenotypes” (R1, R3), “robust leakage-aware validation” (R1, R2), and “comprehensive evaluation” (R1, R2). < Statistical validation of performance gains (R2-W1, Meta) > To statistically validate the reported gains, we performed paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for the overall matched AUC comparisons and paired DeLong tests for disease-level AUC comparisons against MESHAgents under matched evaluation settings. Both our DeepSeek-V3.2-based and GPT-5.1-based agents show significant improvements over MESHAgents, with p less than 0.05 in all tests. We will explicitly clarify the statistical significance of these comparisons in the revised version. < Additional baselines against AutoFE and novelty (R1, R2-W2, Meta) > We agree AutoFE methods such as OpenFE [Zhang et al., 2023] are useful references. However, CPAgents are designed with a different objective from conventional AutoFE pipelines, which typically search shallow algebraic combinations to maximize predictive accuracy on a fixed target. CPAgents are motivated by the construction of clinically interpretable composite phenotypes under explicit validity constraints. Candidate phenotypes are generated within a constrained closed-form operator space and are then filtered through verifier-based checks for physiological plausibility, statistical stability, and cross-classifier consistency. In our evaluation, OpenFE underperformed both baselines, indicating that unconstrained feature generation alone is insufficient for this setting. Directly applying unconstrained algebraic feature search may require additional filtering to ensure unit consistency and valid value ranges for downstream classification. We will make this distinction clearer in the revised version and position AutoFE methods as useful comparative references. < LLM reproducibility (R2-W3)> We agree that unconstrained LLM generation can raise reproducibility concerns. In our framework, however, the LLM is not used as a raw stochastic generator whose outputs are directly evaluated. Instead, it proposes candidate features within a predefined feature space, and each candidate must pass deterministic structural, unit-consistency, and value-range checks before downstream evaluation. Under this fixed validation and evaluation protocol, we report results averaged over five independent seeds, covering both LLM-generation stochasticity and classifier seed variance. The non-zero temperature is used only to diversify candidate proposals, while the retained candidates are governed by the fixed constraints and validation protocol. We will emphasize this constrained generation-and-validation design in the revised version. < Clarification of PheWAS scope, feature dependency, and clinical grounding. (R3-W1/W2/W3) > First, we agree that “PheWAS study” may be ambiguous under the traditional genetic PheWAS definition. Our work does not perform genetic association analysis but a PheWAS-inspired, disease-wide association analysis between cardiovascular imaging-derived phenotypes and clinical outcomes. To avoid confusion, we will revise the terminology to “phenome-wide imaging phenotype association analysis”. Second, we acknowledge that CPAgents operates on pre-extracted imaging-derived features, which is an intentional design choice to ensure interpretability, unit-level validity and fair comparison under a shared feature space. Third, we agree that clinical grounding should be made more explicit. The LLM component is intended to support exploratory hypothesis generation rather than to serve as a standalone source of clinical evidence. We will clarify the current scope and discuss external evidence grounding through curated biomedical literature or clinical guidelines as a future work.

title: CW-B: Class Weighted Boosting Framework for Imbalance Resilient Multi Class Cardiac Phenotyping
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper studies a clinically meaningful problem, namely discharge phenotyping for cardiac conditions where missed detection of certain classes may have downstream implications for management. The task definition and label mapping are clearly presented, and the emphasis on prioritized classes is clinically well motivated. Another strength is that the preprocessing pipeline is described in a leakage-aware and reproducible manner. The manuscript explicitly states that preprocessing statistics are estimated on the training split only, and it augments imputed features with missingness indicators, which is a reasonable design choice for structured clinical data with incomplete documentation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is limited methodological novelty. CW-B appears to be an application of inverse-frequency class weighting on top of XGBoost with standard missingness-indicator augmentation, rather than a substantially new boosting framework. The manuscript presents the method as a novel framework, but the technical contribution seems closer to a well-engineered cost-aware training pipeline than to a new methodological advance. The motivation of handling class imbalance is clinically relevant. However, imbalance-aware learning itself is not new in medical AI, and prior work has already explored data-level correction strategies for imbalanced biomedical classification tasks, e. g. , GAN-based imbalance correction (DiGAN Breakthrough: Advancing diabetic data analysis with innovative GAN-based imbalance correction techniques). In this regard, the present manuscript is better positioned as a task-specific implementation of cost-sensitive tree boosting rather than a substantially new methodological advance. The empirical validation is also not deep enough to isolate the value of each component. There is no ablation showing the effect of class weighting alone, missingness indicators alone, or alternative weighting strategies. This makes it difficult to determine which part of the pipeline is responsible for the observed gains.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) Instead of reporting only overall metrics, the paper performs a detailed analysis of missed detections for clinically important phenotypes (stableCAD, ACS, CAS), providing actionable insights into which classes are most often confused. (2) The framework explicitly handles incomplete documentation and high measurement variability through robust preprocessing (median imputation plus missing indicators) and leverages XGBoost’s native missing‑value handling, making it suitable for noisy, real‑hospital data rather than idealized benchmarks. (3) The ground truth is strengthened by incorporating the Gensini score for disease burden and longitudinal follow‑up for CAD‑related events, improving the reliability of discharge phenotype labels beyond routine administrative codes.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The core technical components class‑weighted XGBoost and missing indicator with median imputation are well‑established practices, offering limited methodological novelty: Assigning instance weights inversely proportional to class frequencies is a native feature of XGBoost. This practice is extensively documented in the official XGBoost documentation and widely used in multi‑class imbalance scenarios. The missing indicator method (MIM) – imputing missing values with a simple statistic (e.g., median) while adding a binary indicator for missingness – is a classical missing data handling strategy. (2) Ablation study for the missingness handling strategy is completely missing, leaving its claimed benefit unsubstantiated: The paper states that explicit missingness modeling (median imputation + missing indicator concatenation) is a key component of the robust training pipeline. However, no ablation experiments are conducted to validate this claim. Specifically, the paper does not compare: Median imputation alone (without missing indicators); Missing indicators alone (with zero or constant imputation); Alternative imputation methods (mean imputation, k‑NN, multiple imputation, or MissForest); No explicit missingness handling (letting XGBoost natively handle missing values by learning the best split direction). (3) The clinical justification for the prioritized class set Cp = {0, 1, 3} (stableCAD, ACS, CAS) is insufficiently argued. The paper defines Cp = {0, 1, 3} as clinically prioritized phenotypes because they are “associated with established diagnostic and therapeutic pathways”. However, the rationale is weakly supported.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This work addresses a clinically important and practically relevant challenge in medical informatics, namely the underrecognition of acute high-risk phenotypes in the presence of class imbalance and incomplete data. The emphasis on minimizing false negatives for high-risk classes is particularly well aligned with clinical priorities, where missed detections can have significant consequences for patient safety and downstream care. A key strength of the paper lies in its focus on interpretability and trustworthiness. By building on XGBoost and emphasizing auditable decision logic, the proposed approach offers greater transparency compared to black-box deep learning models. This is especially valuable in clinical settings, where interpretability is essential for practitioner trust, deployment, and potential regulatory considerations. The paper also demonstrates a strong understanding of real-world data challenges. The explicit handling of missingness, including the use of missingness indicators and structured preprocessing, is well motivated and appropriate for electronic health record (EHR) data, which is often heterogeneous and incomplete. This contributes to the robustness and practical applicability of the proposed framework. Finally, the methodology is clearly presented. The inclusion of a detailed algorithm outlining the integration of class weighting and missingness handling into the boosting framework improves clarity and supports reproducibility. The step-by-step formulation makes it easier for readers to understand and potentially reimplement the approach.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Incremental Methodological Novelty: The core technique of applying class weights to gradient boosting (XGBoost) is a standard feature in existing libraries (e.g., scale_pos_weight or sample weights). While the authors frame this as a “framework” (CW-B), the methodological innovation appears somewhat incremental. The paper needs to clearly distinguish its specific weighting strategy from standard cost-sensitive learning implementations available in off-the-shelf tools. Comparison to State-of-the-Art: The abstract mentions a “unified baseline suite,” but it is not validated by the results, it may have been a small increase of the results, not any major improvement, other complex models will outperform it. Scope of Evaluation: The focus is on “Cardiac Phenotyping,” but the abstract does not specify the granularity of the classes or the exact data source (e.g., specific cohort size or feature dimensions). The generalizability of the specific weighting scheme to other phenotyping tasks remains to be seen.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and all three reviewers for their careful evaluation. We appreciate their recognition of the clinical relevance of reliable cardiovascular discharge phenotyping under real-world class imbalance and missingness, especially for reducing missed detections of stableCAD, ACS, and CAS. CW-B is a clinical risk-aligned phenotyping pipeline that integrates clinical risk prioritization, class-balanced learning, missingness-aware modeling, and classwise error auditing within a unified five-class task. Under a fold-specific, leakage-free protocol, it performs missing-sentinel conversion, training-split-only preprocessing, missingness-indicator augmentation, and class-balanced instance weighting, and evaluates clinically important errors using prioritized recall, F1, miss rate, and confusion-pattern analysis. R1-W1, R2-W1, R3-W1: Novelty and method positioning The novelty of CW-B lies in its risk-aligned formulation for cardiac discharge phenotyping. In this task, different errors have asymmetric clinical consequences, so overall accuracy or generic imbalance handling alone is insufficient. CW-B targets high-risk missed detection by combining fold-specific class-balanced weighting, explicit missingness modeling, and prioritized evaluation of stableCAD, ACS, and CAS. Under the same 5-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, CW-B achieves the strongest or most competitive Accuracy, Macro-F1, Balanced Accuracy, and Prioritized F1 among strong tree-based, ensemble, and neural baselines. Its improvement over a higher-capacity XGBoost baseline further indicates that the gain is not simply due to model capacity. We will clarify this positioning in the revision. R1-W2, R2-W2: Empirical evidence, component contributions, and missingness handling Following the meta-review and the rebuttal policy, we provide preliminary additional ablation results to clarify the contribution of each component. These analyses were conducted under the same 5-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, random seed, and main model configuration. Removing class weighting reduces Macro-F1, Balanced Accuracy, and Prioritized F1 to 0.6968/0.6621/0.6631.Removing the missingness indicator gives 0.6804/0.6666/0.6444.Using only XGBoost native missing handling gives 0.7082/0.6909/0.6780.Alternative imputation strategies with indicators also underperform the main model; for example, KNN yields 0.7008/0.6791/0.6703.These preliminary results support the role of both core components: class-balanced instance weighting improves macro-level and prioritized-class performance, while explicit missingness modeling benefits clinically prioritized phenotypes. Among 4354 samples and 57 features, 55 features contain missing values, with 38571 missing entries out of 248178 total entries, corresponding to a 15.54% missingness rate, suggesting that documentation patterns carry clinically relevant information. In the revision, we will include the finalized ablation table and clarify that all preprocessing statistics are estimated only from the training split. R2-W3, R3-W2: Clinical rationale for $C_p={0,1,3}$ $C_p={0,1,3}$ is a pre-defined clinical-priority set based on clinical actionability and missed-detection risk. ACS is a time-sensitive acute ischemic phenotype; stableCAD informs secondary prevention, medication planning, and follow-up; and CAS in this cohort refers to clinically suspected CAD patients with less than 50% luminal narrowing who still require risk assessment and symptom management. $C_p$ provides a clinical-risk-oriented evaluation perspective without changing the training labels, model objective, or post-processing rules; the model always performs unified five-class prediction. In the revision, we will state earlier that $C_p$ is determined by clinical actionability and missed-detection risk, not by class frequency or experimental results. We thank the reviewers again and will revise the manuscript accordingly.

title: Deep-IMMA: an Interpretable Immune-Aware Multimodal Deep Representation Learning for Cancer Prognosis and Recurrence Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) They have a strong biological motivation focused on tumor–immune microenvironment which is evident through explicit modeling of tissue compartments. 2) They have rich multi-task supervision (segmentation, counts, immune labels, captions) to enrich representations. 3) Their model produces interpretability attention maps of immune infiltration between recurrence and non-recurrence phenotypes. 4) They also combine vision, language, and spatial signals in a unified framework.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) There’s a heavy reliance on expensive supervision, including pixel-level (on tiles) tissue segmentation maps. Additionally, the dice score is very low ~0.22.They argue segmentation is not meant to be precise but “interaction-centric,” but this is not fully convincing. If segmentation is inaccurate, it is unclear how reliable downstream biological supervision is. 2) it is unclear what the role of the Q-former is. While the attention maps are good, have they been evaluated by a pathologist? 3) No external validation: it would be great if this were validated. It is unclear whether the claimed tumor–immune interaction is actually modeled or if the model only learns co-occurrence patterns through shared supervision and spatial proximity. 4) It is unclear what staining or slide type was used. Is it H&E primarily? Why does it say virtual H&E from DAPI? The images seem to be TMA and not biopsy slides. 5) Usually prognostic models are evaluated in terms of C-index, hazard ratio, survival curves. 6) Also unclear where is the structured text from captions coming from?
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Biologically grounded supervision is a compelling idea. Instead of purely morphological features, the framework explicitly encodes immune-tumor spatial interactions (6 immune infiltration phenotypes) as structured supervision signals. This is well-motivated by pathology literature showing immune contexture predicts outcomes. 2.Unified multi-task framework is elegant. Jointly training segmentation, captioning, classification, and regression within a single Stage 1 pipeline with uncertainty-weighted losses is a clean design that avoids training separate models. 3.Thorough ablation study. The paper systematically ablates Stage 1 components (backbone, alignment loss) and Stage 2 components (spatial encoding, Top-K, auxiliary grade, sparsity regularization), with CIs for all results. 5.Practical clinical value. The model works from histology alone (no MRI/genomics), making it more clinically accessible.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.very small dataset and single-site evaluation. Only 212 patients / 711 slides from a single institution. The 95% CI for AUROC is wide (0.666-0.847), and with only 44 test patients, results could be unstable. No external validation on any public prostate cancer dataset (e.g., TCGA-PRAD) is provided. For clinical prognosis claims, multi-site validation is essential. 2.Limited baselines — no comparison with modern pathology VLMs or survival models. The baselines are only Logistic Regression and ABMIL. No comparison with CONCH, PathChat, CLAM, TransMIL, or any recent WSI-level prognosis methods. The claim of outperforming “morphology-only” models lacks comparison with current SOTA slide-level prognosis methods that also use foundation model features. 3.Virtual H&E images (from DAPI/autofluorescence) limit generalizability. The entire pipeline uses virtual H&E converted from fluorescence imaging, not standard H&E. This is a significant limitation for clinical deployment since most pathology labs use conventional H&E staining. The paper does not discuss or validate whether the learned representations transfer to real H&E. 4.U-net decoder architecture is underspecified. Critically, the paper does not specify which intermediate ViT layers from the frozen UNI backbone provide skip connections to the U-net decoder, how many skip connections are used, or the decoder architecture details (layers, channels). Or do you directly use Qformer semantic ebmeddings for segmentation? how do you do that? Since standard ViTs lack the natural multi-scale feature hierarchies of CNNs, how skip connections are constructed for a U-net decoder from a ViT is a non-trivial design choice that directly impacts segmentation quality — and this is entirely undocumented, hindering reproducibility. 5.No survival analysis or time-to-event modeling — binary BCR classification discards censored data. BCR prediction is framed as binary classification rather than survival analysis (Cox regression, C-index), which is the standard approach for recurrence prediction in oncology. This is a significant methodological limitation: the paper mentions excluding slides that “lacked BCR labels,” but in clinical practice many patients are censored (lost to follow-up or have not yet recurred at the time of data collection). Binary classification forces exclusion of censored patients, wasting valuable data and potentially introducing selection bias. Survival analysis methods (e.g., Cox proportional hazards, discrete-time survival models) naturally handle censoring and provide time-to-event predictions that are more clinically actionable than binary yes/no recurrence labels. 6.Batch size for Stage 1 multi-task training is not reported — a critical omission for the InfoNCE alignment loss. The paper does not report the training batch size for Stage 1.While the segmentation, classification, and regression losses work well with small batches, the InfoNCE contrastive alignment loss (L_align) is known to be highly sensitive to batch size. Without knowing the batch size, it is impossible to assess whether the contrastive alignment is properly trained or undertrained, and the result cannot be reproduced.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The focus on immune-aware representation learning is well-motivated and clinically relevant. 2.The use of structured supervision provides a biologically grounded learning signal. 3.The framework produces interpretable outputs, including attention maps and immune patterns. 4.The two-stage design is reasonable and supported by ablation studies.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty is moderate. The framework primarily integrates existing components. 2.The multi-task objective is complex, and the relative contribution of individual supervision signals is not fully analyzed. 3.Baseline comparisons could be stronger, particularly with more recent pathology foundation models. 4.Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative and would benefit from more rigorous validation.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and Area Chair for the constructive feedback. Below, we clarify points that may have led to ambiguity in the manuscript. 1.Implementation Details and Architecture (R1, R2, R3): Stage 1 of our model uses the UNI vision transformer backbone. For segmentation, visual tokens from blocks 3, 6, and 9 are reshaped into spatial maps and projected to 256, 128, and 64 channels, respectively, before being used as decoder skip features. The Q-Former is a compact semantic bottleneck for vision-text alignment: 64 learnable queries attend over image tokens, and the query features are used for auxiliary prediction, image-text alignment, and downstream aggregation. Batch sizes were 32 (Stage 1) and 4 (Stage 2). 2.Data Representation, Captions, and Domain Gap (R1, R2, MR): The image data consist of prostate tissue microarray (TMA) cores rather than whole biopsy-slide WSIs. Each core includes virtual H&E/histology images generated from DAPI/autofluorescence imaging, paired single-cell-derived tissue maps, immune phenotypes, and structured captions. Captions are rule-based summaries from the single-cell table, including cell counts, cell-type abundance levels, and immune-infiltration phenotypes; they are not free-form manual annotations or generated text. Regarding the virtual H&E domain gap, Deep-IMMA builds on UNI, pretrained on large-scale real H&E WSIs, including prostate pathology data. We agree that real H&E validation would further strengthen generalizability. 3.Survival Analysis and Risk Stratification (R1, R2, MR): We acknowledge that time-to-event modeling and C-index evaluation are clinically important for predicting recurrence, especially in the presence of censoring. In this study, recurrence prediction was formulated as binary BCR classification to evaluate immune-aware representation learning under a controlled patient-level split. Stage 2 MIL model outputs a continuous recurrence probability, interpretable as a risk score for stratifying recurrence phenotypes. Thus, current results demonstrate risk-discrimination capability, while survival modeling with censoring is outside the scope of the current project. 4.Segmentation Dice and Biological Supervision Reliability (R1, R2): We agree that the segmentation branch should not be interpreted as a high-accuracy standalone segmentation model. Its role is an auxiliary spatial/semantic anchor for tissue composition and tumor–immune topology, not pixel-perfect boundaries. Structured captions and immune-phenotype labels are derived from single-cell/tissue annotations rather than from predicted segmentation maps. Thus, low boundary-level DICE values do not directly imply that immune supervision itself is unreliable. Ablations in Table 2 suggest that spatially structured supervision and aggregation contribute to discrimination of recurrence risk. 5.Interpretability (R3, MR): We present attention and immune-pattern maps as evidence. The maps highlight regions with immune-infiltration patterns consistent with known tumor–immune dynamics and help examine which tissue regions contribute to recurrence prediction. Pathologist assessment would further strengthen this interpretation. 6.Baselines Comparison and Contribution (R2, R3, MR) Broader benchmarking would further strengthen the study. The submitted experiments compare pathology foundation backbones, including UNI, Prov-GigaPath, and H-optimus-0, and evaluate recurrence prediction against logistic regression and ABMIL with targeted ablations (Table 1,2). These analyses were designed to isolate the effects of immune-structured supervision and spatial aggregation within the same patient-level split, rather than to provide exhaustive benchmarking. The main contribution is injecting tumor-relative immune topology into foundation-model adaptation, enabling H&E-only risk discrimination and spatial interpretation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This work proposes a multimodal, immune-aware framework for prostate cancer recurrence prediction that combines structured supervision signals, vision-language alignment, and spatial MIL aggregation to learn biologically informed representations from histopathology. Reviewers consistently acknowledge that the problem is clinically meaningful and that the attempt to explicitly model tumor–immune microenvironment interactions is a strong and relevant motivation. The overall pipeline is well-structured and demonstrates thoughtful integration of multiple supervision sources, with the potential to support more interpretable prognostic modeling. The use of histology-only inputs for inference is also noted as a practical advantage. At the same time, there is a shared concern that the methodological novelty of the work is limited. The proposed approach largely integrates existing components, including multitask learning, vision-language feature alignment, and MIL-based aggregation, into a unified pipeline. While this combination is reasonable and well-engineered, it is not yet fully clear what fundamentally new learning principle or architectural contribution is introduced beyond this integration. There are also concerns regarding the strength and clarity of the experimental validation. The study is conducted on a relatively small, single-institution cohort, which limits confidence in generalization. Several reviewers also note that the evaluation would benefit from stronger comparison against more recent pathology foundation models and more clinically standard prognostic frameworks. In addition, the use of a binary recurrence formulation instead of time-to-event survival modeling raises questions about clinical completeness, as it discards censoring information that is typically important in oncological prognosis. Another recurring point is the limited clarity around certain components of the framework. In particular, the role and construction of structured textual supervision, the reliability and interpretation of immune-related annotations, and the relative contribution of each supervision signal are not fully disentangled. This makes it difficult to assess how much of the reported performance gain is driven by biologically meaningful learning versus correlated supervision or model scaling effects. Interpretability claims based on attention maps are also viewed as promising but would benefit from more rigorous validation. Overall, the submission addresses an important clinical problem and presents a well-motivated multimodal learning framework with clear practical relevance. Despite limitations in novelty and validation breadth, the work is solid, clinically grounded, and of interest to the community. With improved clarity and stronger experimental support, it could represent a meaningful contribution.

title: DIVER-Surv: Diffusion and Virtual-Node Graph Fusion for Cross-Cohort Glioma Survival
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Interaction-Aware Multimodal Fusion: The framework utilizes an attention-based graph with a learnable virtual node to capture complex, non-linear interactions between mpMRI sequences and clinical context. This architecture surpasses standard concatenation methods by enabling sample-specific message passing, which refines global patient representations and maintains significant risk-group separation even under institutional domain shift. 2.Harmonization-Free Clinical Encoding: By converting heterogeneous clinical variables into natural-language summaries via an LLM and encoding them with a frozen biomedical language model, the authors provide a practical solution to inconsistent data naming across cohorts. This approach demonstrates strong clinical feasibility, allowing the model to integrate diverse institutional data without requiring manual covariate alignment or site-specific feature engineering.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The dual-branch 3D diffusion-based objective significantly increases computational overhead, yet the authors do not provide a detailed analysis of training time or memory requirements compared to standard models. Additionally, while an LLM summarizes clinical data, there is no formal verification process to ensure the accuracy of these narrative outputs or to check for potential information loss during the text generation phase. 2.Data Constraints and Resolution Limitations: The evaluation relies on the RHUH-GBM cohort, which consists of only 40 patients, limiting the statistical power for external validation. Furthermore, resizing all MRI volumes to 120x120x64 may discard high-resolution phenotypic features essential for precise glioma prognosis and risk stratification.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper focuses on a clinically significant topic: the limited generalisability of survival prediction models across institutions due to variations in imaging acquisition protocols and heterogeneous clinical data. 2.This paper proposed a clinically practical framework to encode clinical data and mpMRI. Instead of using diffusion for image generation, the model leverages denoising objectives and consistency regularization to learn acquisition-invariant features, which is particularly relevant for handling inter-site variability in medical imaging. 3.The paper includes rigorous cross-cohort evaluation protocol. The model is trained on a single institution and tested on independent external datasets, providing a realistic assessment of generalization performance under domain shift. 4.The paper includes comprehensive ablation studies that systematically evaluate the contribution of each component, including imaging, clinical encoding, and fusion strategies.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Lack of methodological novelty: while the overall framework is well-designed, the individual components （including diffusion-based representation learning, LLM-based clinical encoding, and graph-based fusion) are not novel on their own. The main contribution lies in their integration rather than a fundamentally new methodological advance. 2.Result not consistently the best: the proposed method does not consistently outperform all baselines across evaluation settings. For instance, in some cross-cohort scenarios, competing methods (e.g., DeepHit) achieve higher C-index values. Although the authors argue comparable clinical stratification, the lack of consistent superiority weakens the overall claim of improved performance. 3.The transformation of structured clinical variables into text representations introduces additional complexity, yet the benefits over standard tabular encoding are not sufficiently justified. It remains unclear whether this step improves performance or introduces potential noise. Ablation test on standard tabular encoding (ML methods) should be applied and compared. 4.Limited interpretability: despite targeting a clinically relevant task, the model lacks interpretability analysis, such as feature attribution, modality importance, or case-level explanations. This limits the transparency and potential clinical adoption of the method.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper has a rigorous setup where external cohorts are never used for hyperparameter tuning or model selection, and evaluates in both directions (UCSF -> UPENN/RHUH and UPENN -> UCSF/RHUH). Including the small RHUH cohort (n=40) as an external stress test adds to this result. 2.The paper reports C-index with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, hazard ratios, and log-rank p-values. Kaplan-Meier curves are provided for qualitative assessment of risk stratification. This is quite comprehensive, which reinforces confidence in the evaluation 3.Table 2 isolates the contribution of each component and shows that each addition contributes incrementally to both internal and external performance. The ablation is well-structured and clearly presented.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The total evaluation involves roughly 1200 patients across three cohorts. While cross-cohort evaluation is rigorous in design, the small sample sizes limit the statistical power of the reported confidence intervals and p-values. The wide CIs on RHUH cohort (eg 0.504 - 0.753) make it difficult to draw strong conclusions about generalization. The paper would benefit from adding more cohorts or adding a discussion on the statistical limitations arising from these sample sizes. 2.The imaging ablation study (Table 2, row 2) uses a diffusion-guided encoder, but the comparison baselines (DeepSurv, DeepHit) replace diffusion with a standard MSE reconstruction loss. The paper does not isolate whether these gains come specifically from the denoising diffusion objective or simply from having any self-supervised regularization on the encoder. An ablation comparing diffusion denoising against other self-supervised objectives (e.g., contrastive learning, masked autoencoding) on the same backbone would clarify this. 3.The clinical text summaries are generated using Gemini 2.0 Flash, a proprietary model whose outputs may change across API versions. This makes it hard to reproduce, as different runs or future replication attempts could produce significantly different patient summaries, which would propagate to different clinical embeddings.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The method is well-motivated and solid. The novelty is moderate, as it mainly integrates existing components and shows some variability in performance across settings. Concerns remain regarding limited interpretability, small external cohort size, and insufficient justification of proposed components.

title: EmERGE: A Multimodal LLM-Based Evidence-Mediated ECG Report Generation and Evaluation Approach
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Clinically meaningful problem formulation: The paper addresses an important weakness of existing ECG report generation systems: they may produce fluent reports without demonstrating that the conclusions are grounded in electrophysiological evidence. Reframing the task around explicit evidence extraction is well motivated and clinically sensible. 2) Interpretable intermediate representation: The use of six structured ECG evidence dimensions is a strong design choice. It aligns with how cardiologists reason about ECGs and provides a more auditable interface than direct end-to-end text generation. 3) Interesting evaluation beyond surface-level text metrics: The rule-guided counterfactual protocol is a meaningful addition. In particular, evaluating Targeted Sensitivity, Non-target Invariance, and Diagnosis Response Consistency goes beyond standard report-generation metrics and attempts to probe whether the model’s diagnostic behavior is causally aligned with waveform evidence. 4) Consistent empirical gains across multiple protocols: The method improves over strong baselines not only on LLM-based clinical metrics (e. g. , AccD, Rel, Fid), but also on classification-oriented metrics (macro/micro F1) and counterfactual consistency measures. This makes the overall empirical case stronger than if only one metric family had improved. 5) Cross-backbone applicability within the tested setting: The framework is evaluated with two representative backbones, PULSE and GEM, and yields gains in both cases. This suggests that the approach is not narrowly tied to one specific model implementation. 6) Clinical relevance: Improving evidence grounding and interpretability is highly relevant for eventual real-world deployment of ECG reporting systems, where unsupported but plausible-sounding conclusions are particularly problematic.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) Methodological novelty is stronger in formulation than in implementation: While the use of structured ECG evidence as an intermediate representation is novel and meaningful in this application domain, the underlying machinery—multi-round prompting, staged generation, and conditioning on intermediate text—is still relatively close to existing multi-step LLM reasoning patterns. The manuscript would be stronger if it more clearly distinguished what is conceptually new from what is inherited from general LLM prompting practice. 2) Dependence on LLM-generated supervision: The structured evidence annotations are partially constructed using GPT-4o together with machine measurements. This is practical, but the paper does not sufficiently analyse how noisy or biased these pseudo-labels may be, nor how sensitive the final system is to errors in this supervision. 3) Counterfactual perturbation realism is not fully established: The counterfactual evaluation is one of the most interesting parts of the paper, but also one of the least fully validated. It is not entirely clear whether the proposed signal-level interventions always correspond to physiologically realistic ECG changes, and therefore how strongly one can interpret these results as evidence of true causal validity. 4) Evaluation emphasis remains skewed toward LLM-derived scores: Although the paper reports classification and counterfactual metrics in addition to LLM-based clinical evaluation, the headline improvements are primarily emphasized through LLM-derived scores. A more balanced presentation of the non-LLM evaluation results would strengthen the empirical claims. 5) Limited failure-mode analysis: The qualitative examples are helpful, but the manuscript does not provide a sufficiently systematic breakdown of where the method still fails. For example, it would be useful to disentangle errors caused by incorrect evidence extraction from those caused by evidence-to-diagnosis reasoning. 6) Reproducibility details are incomplete at the current stage: Although the authors state that code will be released after acceptance, the manuscript does not disclose important implementation details such as the exact prompt templates, evidence-extraction criteria, or thresholding decisions used in constructing the six-dimensional evidence space. These omissions make exact replication difficult. 7) Reference formatting is inconsistent and should be carefully audited: Several citations appear to correspond to recent preprints, but they are not consistently identified as such, and some entries lack clear bibliographic details such as venue information or arXiv identifiers. This does not affect the core technical contribution, but it reduces clarity and makes it harder to assess the status and maturity of the cited prior work. The authors should carefully revise the bibliography and clearly distinguish peer-reviewed publications from preprints.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper evaluates the model across multiple reasonable and clinically relevant scenarios and tasks, comparing it with other baselines. 2.If released, the GPT-4o-generated evidence/reasoning data could be useful for the community. 3.The design and implementation of the counterfactual evaluation are well-motivated and technically sound, apart from some details mentioned below.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While there are many works aiming to generate ECG reports from signals, and this work proposes a structured reasoning approach, I do not fully understand the motivation. In clinical practice, ECG reports are typically generated by rule-based systems embedded in ECG machines. Since the model is trained on these reports as ground truth, it effectively learns to approximate them. What is the advantage of this approach compared to existing rule-based systems, which are simpler and do not hallucinate? 2.In Section 2.2, please define what h(⋅) represents. Is it an LLM? 3.It would be much clearer if the authors explicitly showed how the structured evidence E looks. Is each Ei a single label (Normal / Abnormal / Borderline), or a richer textual description? Also, how are these labels assigned to each phenotype? What cutoffs are used? Following this, why is GPT-4o used to construct E* if the representation is structured and could potentially be formed manually with regex? 4.How were the 12,000 MIMIC-IV and 6,000 PTB-XL samples selected (randomly?), and what is their class distribution? Could happen that most cases are normal. I guess using a smaller sample size was due to GPT-4o API limits and costs, but this can be avoided. 5.In Section 2.2, both Le and Lr appear to be cross-entropy losses, but different notations are used (CE vs. −logp). Why is this inconsistent? Also, the formula formatting is broken. More importantly, is Lr conditioned on predicted E or ground-truth E* during training? 6.For the counterfactual analysis, the perturbations are not clearly described. What exactly are “relevant” and “irrelevant” perturbations? How are they applied? For the DRC metric, what representation or encoder is used to compute delta(D) and delta(E)? 7.Why is a single projector used for both ECG signals and images? Since these are different modalities, a separate design would seem more natural. 8.The implementation details are insufficient. Which LLM is used? Which parts are trained or frozen? Is full fine-tuning performed? How is catastrophic forgetting addressed? Referring to another paper for core details makes reproduction difficult. 9.Evaluation details are unclear. For LLM-based evaluation: which LLM is used, and what are the exact inputs? Why do the reported metrics differ from those in the GEM paper? 10.For CE-based diagnostic accuracy: which labels are used, and how are they extracted from generated reports (e.g., rule-based or regex-based)? 11.In Figure 3, it would be helpful to show the actual ECG signal (e.g., Lead II) for better interpretation. 12.The core idea is similar to reasoning with LLMs. Why not incorporate reasoning directly into supervision and train the model in a single stage instead of a two-step pipeline?
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Here are the major strengths I see in this paper. [S1] The six evidence dimensions are clinically well grounded. They follow the way cardiologists actually read an ECG, going through rhythm, P wave, PR interval, QRS, ST segment, and T wave with QT. Because of this, the intermediate representation is not an arbitrary engineering choice. It reflects real clinical practice, which makes the whole framework easier to trust from a clinician’s point of view. [S2] The causal framing is not just narrated, it is enforced by the design. The model has to produce evidence first in Step 1, and the diagnosis is only allowed in Step 2.The training loss also supervises the evidence before the report. This structurally blocks a common failure mode where the model decides the diagnosis first and then invents matching evidence. This is a small but important design decision. [S3] The counterfactual evaluation is the most original part of the paper. Most ECG report generation works only check text or label accuracy, so it is hard to tell if the model is really using the ECG evidence. Here the authors change specific parts of the signal and watch how the model reacts. They look at three things, targeted sensitivity, non-target invariance, and diagnosis response consistency. The LAFB experiment is especially convincing. When the key evidence is removed, EmERGE drops the diagnosis, while the baseline mostly does not.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: [W1] The automated numbers and the human scores do not match. The abstract claims big improvements, and Table 1 looks good on LLM-based metrics. But in Table 6, EmERGE scores 3.92 on Overall Satisfaction, while GPT-4o scores 4.38 and DeepSeek-R1 scores 4.44.The same pattern shows up in Analytical Relevance, Analytical Accuracy, and Reasoning Quality. So on every item rated by real cardiologists, EmERGE is below the two LLM baselines. The text only says cardiologists rated EmERGE positively, and never mentions this gap. The setup is also a bit confusing. Section 3.5 says GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 were used as ground truth, but the same two models still appear with their own scores in Table 6.Why did the authors not discuss this gap or clarify the evaluation setup? [W2] The six evidence labels are made by GPT-4o and featureDB, and the whole method is trained on these labels. But no cardiologist ever checks whether the labels are actually correct. There is no verified subset and no agreement score with human experts. GPT-4o is a general language model, not an ECG specialist, and featureDB gives machine-based features. If the labels are off in some systematic way, every claim about causal grounding is also off. The authors mention this in one line at the end, but the whole method rests on this supervision. Why did the authors not include a cardiologist-verified subset or report inter-rater agreement?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Meta Reviewer and all reviewers for your professional comments. Below, we shall clarify your key concerns. 1.Research Motivation (R2.1) Traditional rule-based ECG methods are simple to implement and can generate plausible reports in routine cases. However, they rely heavily on predefined rules and are sensitive to signal quality. They fail in cases with severe waveform noise or complex comorbidities. To address these limitations, data-driven deep learning methods have been developed for ECG report generation (please see DOI: 10.1038/s41467-020-15432-4 for reference). They outperform conventional rule-based baselines consistently. EmERGE targets grounded reports by linking waveform patterns to diagnostic conclusions via interpretable evidence. Experimental results further verify that our evidence-driven approach surpasses end-to-end methods, achieving a 13% improvement in the CE metric. 2.Supervision and Expert Validation (R1.2, 1.4, 3.1, 3.2) We clarify potential misunderstandings in experimental settings. Our framework builds upon LLM-based generation and evaluation; thus, we conduct human expert assessment in Table 6.GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 are not used as comparative baselines. They serve only to validate the quality of silver labels adopted for EmERGE training. Strong performance of GPT-4o confirms that our supervisory signals are clinically reliable and free of systematic bias. Intermediate features extracted by FeatureDB are derived from validated rule-based beat-level algorithms in prior studies. The LLM acts merely as a reasoning engine. Nevertheless, Table 6 provides solid indirect evidence to support the reliability of our framework. 3.Counterfactual Intervention (R1.3, 2.6) Due to page limits, the initial submission lacks complete elaboration on rule-based interventions, which may cause ambiguity. We will supplement more details in the camera-ready version. Our rule-based interventions guarantee clinical plausibility. Rules are defined as structured operations on specific leads and segments toward predefined clinical goals. We define two intervention types: Targeted Intervention: expected to alter diagnostic conclusions; Non-Target Intervention: expected to preserve original diagnoses. The intervention replaces segmented waveforms with normal templates at the beat level, followed by smoothing and cropping. All rules are formulated based on official AHA and Philips guidelines. Interventions are deterministically executed via Neurokit2 at the signal level, effectively mitigating LLM hallucinations. This protocol examines whether the model truly relies on clinical evidence for diagnosis. We acknowledge that real-world distribution and clinical alignment require further validation, which we will in our future work. 4.Dataset Configuration (R2.4) For fair comparison with baseline methods, we adopt the same data split ratio as GEM. We select a smaller training set for few-shot learning and verify our structural evidence-driven approach. By explicitly grounding report generation on structured clinical evidence, our method outperforms GEM with far less training data (18k vs. 120k). This outcome demonstrates that our evidence-driven paradigm extracts denser and more effective supervision signals than vanilla end-to-end learning. We will continue to adopt larger datasets in future optimizations. 5.Definition of Six-Dimensional Features (R1.6, 2.3) Following AHA guidelines, we define six feature dimensions covering rhythm, P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment, and T wave & QT interval. Each dimension employs semi-structured natural language descriptions. Every entry contains a categorical label (Normal, Abnormal, or Borderline) and a concise textual characterization, without involving final diagnostic judgments.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This is an quite novel study to reformulate ECG interpretation as a two-step reasoning process to make diagnosis with explicit clinical evidence.

title: Fibers of Asymmetric Similarity: A Framework for Clinical and Imaging Data
reviewer_1_strengths: The whole idea is interesting and seems to work well. In particular, I find what is shown in Fig. 4 particularly valid: classification performance using feature extracted by pre-trained backbones (e. g. , DINOv2b or BioMedCLIP) improves by up to 4X (F1@0.5), notably, without fine-tuning. The authors achieve this impressive results by optimizing the only learnable entities in the image processing pipeline, i. e. , class prototypes (as per the paper, CxMxD parameters, 5x256 per class) and projection layers (about which no information is given, but presumably very lightweight, too). This achievement is coupled and justified by the choice to use prototype learning instead of traditional one-hot encoded classification.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper is not particularly clear. 1a. The first line of the abstract introduces the problems related to prenatal screening for CHD, but the end of the abstract is about thyroid nodule classification. Overall, the paper suggests that the authors dealt with CHD detection, but then thyroid nodules appear out of nowhere. In my humble opinion, a clearer way to present the work would be to introduce the actual clinical tasks and datasets at the very end, and to be more general about asymmetry and rare conditions in the introduction/abstract, but then the authors should address the lack of comparison or context for the second task (see point 1e). Maybe it would be better not to include the thyroid-related task altogether, as its results 1b. In Method, the authors talk about “clinical data” and “features”, so I assume that we are talking about tabular data (also because in Introduction the authors wrote “structured clinical data”), but this is opaque. Then, the reader is given no information about what the authors define “independent clinical parameters (e. g. , blood pressure)” and “relational or interdependent features”. Since the work gives a great importance to this division, I think the reader would benefit from a clear explanation of why this was necessary. Also, as per 2.1, we know that “temporal or repeated measurements (e. g. , gestational age)” are “embedded and pooled as h”, D-dimensional embeddings, but then what about the rest of data (i. e. , non-temporal but independent features and interdependent features)? 1c. The framework is presented as “unified”, but in fact clinical data and images are treated separately by separate models, right?
